newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU treaty talks fail to lay ground for enlargement.
newsitem.headline: EU treaty talks fail to lay ground for enlargement.

text.p: The European Union failed on Wednesday to agree key reforms to expand into eastern Europe and looked set to agree a new treaty that was a shadow of what many in the 15-nation bloc had hoped for.

Working late into the night, EU leaders threw in the towel on plans to alter the balance of power within the Union, deferring the issue until just before the first of a raft of new members from the old Communist bloc is due to join.
One EU diplomat said the leaders had no appetite for a long drawn out fight after two days of talks that had already scaled back a treaty to meet national sensitivities.
Officials said Belgium and Spain had refused to agree a plan under which the number of votes given to countries in ministerial meetings would be changed to rebalance the power of larger countries.
Belgium objected to seeing The Netherlands get more votes while Spain saw its status as one of the bloc's large countries being diminished.
The treaty -- and particularly the now disbanded streamlining of decision-making procedures -- was seen as crucial to preparing for some dozen new members over the next decade.
Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Romania, Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovenia and Cyprus have all been told they can join the western club.
The failure added to the EU's woes at a summit dominated initially by a row between France and Germany over economic control after the introduction of a single currency.
Although the currency row was smoothed over on Monday with a compromise, it was widely seen as just papering over a huge political divide that would likely re-open.
The long treaty negotiations leading up to the summit had already toned down much of what the bloc had hoped to achieve in terms of signalling a new Citizens' Europe for the next century.
The talks on Monday and Tuesday continued the process.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair, worried about undermining NATO's role, effectively vetoed the idea of incorporating the Western European Union (WEU) defence arm into the bloc.
The treaty simply recognised a "possibility" that it would happen one day.
A Franco-German-led group had wanted to fully integrate the WEU into the Union to build a European defence architecture alongside the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
But Britain, backed for different reasons by Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Austria and Ireland, warned this could undermine NATO's position as Europe's security bedrock.

Grand designs to appoint a senior figure to give a single face and voice to a credible common European foreign policy also came to little, with the 15 leaders set to give a little-known Eurocrat the job of representing the Union in foreign policy.
In areas likely to be hailed by leaders as a success, the summit agreed that EU countries would cooperate more closely on asylum, immigration, visa policy and crime fighting.
But even here there were setbacks. Germany refused to give up its veto on asylum policy.
Britain, Ireland and Denmark also secured opt-outs from various moves to beef up cooperation on borders and immigration is part of the EU's plans to create an area of freedom, security and justice.
The plan was designed to appeal to citizens who are turning away from the bloc because of austerity programmes needed to get monetary union off its planned January 1999 launch-pad.
Leaders had earlier agreed to insert an employment chapter into the new treaty, providing for incentive measures to boost cooperation on employment between member states.
